lookForward.fits: The red deer rut peaks in the first days of October; this is the weekend to go, and it is free everywhere.
lookForward.headline: The deer rut: go at dawn this weekend
lookForward.line: Red deer stags roar and clash all October. Best in the first hour of light: Richmond and Bushy Park in London, Bradgate near Leicester, Exmoor. Stay 50 metres back, dogs on leads, use zoom not feet.

source.name: The Royal Parks: Deer safety advice

more: The rut is the deer breeding season. For a few weeks the stags stop grazing quietly and spend the day bellowing, walking in parallel with rivals, thrashing bracken with their antlers and occasionally locking them with a crack you can hear across a field. It peaks around the start of October and is over by early November.

Go at first light. The deer are most active then, the parks are almost empty, and the low sun and mist do the rest. Richmond Park and Bushy Park in London open at 7am for cars and are free; Bradgate Park near Leicester, Tatton in Cheshire, Lyme in Greater Manchester and the open moor on Exmoor all have wild or park herds.

The safety part matters, and the parks repeat it every autumn. Keep at least 50 metres away. Never walk between two stags, never get between a stag and his hinds, and never try for a closer photograph; use whatever zoom you have. Keep dogs on a lead, or better, walk them somewhere else this month. If a deer looks at you and starts walking over, back away slowly. Do not run, shout or wave.
Take a flask. Stand still in one place for twenty minutes rather than walking about, and the field will fill up around you.

goodThing.fits: National Poetry Day is today, Thursday 1 October 2026, across the UK.
goodThing.headline: A whole country reading poems out loud today
goodThing.line: National Poetry Day is today, and 1.5 million people take part: schools, libraries, buses, radio. The theme is wonder. Read one poem aloud.

source.name: Forward Arts Foundation: National Poetry Day

more: National Poetry Day falls on the first Thursday in October and is run by the Forward Arts Foundation, the charity behind the Forward Prizes. Around 1.5 million people take part each year, which makes it the biggest mass celebration of poetry in the country.

Each year has a one-word theme, and this year it is wonder. Libraries put up displays and hand out free poems, schools spend a lesson on it, bookshops hold readings, and poems turn up in places that are not books: on buses, in hospital corridors, read out on the radio between the news and the weather.

You do not need an event. The whole thing works at the kitchen table. Find one short poem, read it out loud to whoever is in the room, and then read it a second time, because almost nobody hears a poem the first time. If you have children, let them choose; children pick by sound, which is the right way to pick.

If you want a poem for this year's theme and today's weather, look for Gerard Manley Hopkins, who wrote about ordinary dappled things as if they were miracles, or Mary Oliver, who wrote short poems about mornings outside. Both are easy to find free online.

onThisDay.fits: 1 October 1971: the first CT scan of a patient, at Atkinson Morley Hospital in Wimbledon, London.
onThisDay.headline: A machine looked inside a living head
onThisDay.line: Doctors at Atkinson Morley Hospital in Wimbledon made the first CT scan of a patient. Its engineer, Godfrey Hounsfield, won a Nobel Prize in 1979.

source.name: IEEE Engineering and Technology History Wiki: First CT Scanner, 1971

funFact.fits: Conkers are falling under the horse chestnuts all over Britain this week.
funFact.statement: Conkers, the shiny brown nuts under horse chestnut trees, are safe to eat.
funFact.reveal: They are mildly poisonous to people and dogs. Play with them, thread them on string, but do not cook them.

calmRead.fits: Expands today's On this day: the first CT scan of a patient, Wimbledon, 1 October 1971.
calmRead.title: The scanner that came from a record company
calmRead.teaser: Fifty-five years ago today, a machine in Wimbledon looked inside a living head.
paragraphs: On 1 October 1971, a woman with a suspected brain tumour lay very still inside a strange grey box at Atkinson Morley Hospital in Wimbledon, south London. The machine moved around her head a step at a time, taking X-ray readings from every angle. The scan took about five minutes. The numbers went off to a large computer at a laboratory in Hayes, west London, and two days later the radiologist, James Ambrose, was handed the picture: a dark circle, exactly where he had suspected a cyst.

Until that morning, a doctor who wanted to see inside a living skull had very little to work with. An ordinary X-ray goes through soft tissue and shows almost nothing of the brain. The alternatives were unpleasant and risky. Now there was a photograph.

The engineer who built the machine was Godfrey Hounsfield, a farmer's son from Nottinghamshire who had learned electronics with the RAF during the war and had never been to university. He worked for EMI, a company far better known for making records. The Beatles were on its label, and the money coming in gave its research laboratory room to let engineers follow odd ideas.

Hounsfield's odd idea had come to him on a country walk: if you measured a box from enough directions, could a computer work out what was inside? It could. A South African physicist, Allan Cormack, had worked out much of the mathematics separately. The two shared the Nobel Prize in 1979.
A scan today takes a second, and millions of people have had one. It started here, fifty-five years ago this morning.

source.name: IEEE Engineering and Technology History Wiki: First CT Scanner, 1971

word.fits: National Poetry Day, and the English word for the first week of October.
word.meaning: Soft, ripe, unhurried. Keats opened his autumn poem with mists and mellow fruitfulness, and October in Britain has looked like that ever since.

kindness.text: Send someone four lines of a poem you like, with no explanation. Nobody has ever minded receiving one.

joke.setup: Why do stags roar all through October?
joke.punchline: Because it is cheaper than buying flowers, and it carries further.

riddle.riddle: I fall in a spiky green case, I shine for one day and go dull, and children fight duels with me on a string. What am I?
